replacement: As it happened, the boy’s relatives on his mother’s side forgot him too, at first. His grandfather was dead. His widow, Mitya’s grandmother, had moved to Moscow and was gravely ill. The daughters were all married. So for almost a year Mitya stayed with old Grigory and lived with him in the servant’s cottage. Even if his father had remembered him (he could hardly have been altogether unaware that the boy existed), he would have sent him back to the cottage anyway, since a child would only have got in the way of his debauchery. Then a cousin of Mitya’s mother, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, returned from Paris. He lived abroad for many years afterwards, but at that time he was quite a young man and stood out among the Miüsovs as a man of enlightened ideas and European culture, who had lived in the capitals and abroad. Late in life he became a Liberal of the kind common in the forties and fifties. Over his career he had met many of the most Liberal men of his day, in Russia and abroad. He had known Proudhon and Bakunin personally. In his old age he loved to describe the three days of the Paris Revolution of February 1848, hinting that he had very nearly fought on the barricades himself. It was one of the fondest memories of his youth. He owned an independent property of about a thousand souls, reckoning in the old way. His splendid estate lay on the edge of our little town and bordered the lands of our famous monastery. Almost as soon as he inherited it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch started an endless lawsuit against the monastery over fishing rights in the river or wood-cutting in the forest, I don’t know which. He saw it as his duty, as a citizen and a man of culture, to open an attack on the “clericals.” He heard the whole story of Adelaïda Ivanovna, whom, of course, he remembered, and in whom he had once taken an interest. When he learned that Mitya existed, he stepped in, for all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovitch. He met Fyodor Pavlovitch for the first time and told him bluntly that he wanted to take over the child’s education. Long afterwards he used to tell, as a telling detail, that when he began to speak of Mitya, Fyodor Pavlovitch stared for some time as if he didn’t understand which child was meant, and even seemed surprised to hear he had a little son in the house. The story may be exaggerated, but it must have been something like the truth.

As it turned out, the old lady died soon afterward, but in her will she left the boys a thousand roubles each “for their instruction, and so that all be spent on them exclusively, with the condition that it be so portioned out as to last till they are twenty-one, for it is more than adequate provision for such children. If other people think fit to throw away their money, let them.” I have not read the will myself, but I heard that there was something odd of the kind in it, very whimsically worded. The main heir was Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the Marshal of Nobility of the province, and he proved to be an honest man. He wrote to Fyodor Pavlovitch and saw right away that there was nothing to be got out of him for the children’s education. (Fyodor Pavlovitch never actually said no, but only stalled, as he always did in such cases, and was even, at times, gushingly sentimental.) So Yefim Petrovitch took an interest in the orphans himself. He grew especially fond of the younger one, Alexey, who lived for a long time as a member of his family. I ask the reader to note this from the start. The young people owed their schooling and upbringing to Yefim Petrovitch more than to anyone else. He was a man of a generosity and humanity one rarely meets. He left the two thousand roubles that the general’s widow had left them untouched, so that by the time they came of age, the interest had doubled their shares. He paid for both their educations out of his own pocket, and he certainly spent far more than a thousand roubles on each. I will not give a detailed account of their boyhood and youth, only a few of the most important events. About the elder, Ivan, I will say only that he grew into a rather sullen, reserved boy, though far from timid. At ten he had understood that they lived not in their own home but on other people’s charity, and that their father was a man it was shameful to speak of. From very early on, almost from infancy (so they say, at least), the boy showed a brilliant and unusual talent for learning. I don’t know exactly why, but he left Yefim Petrovitch’s family when he was barely thirteen, and went to a Moscow gymnasium, where he boarded with an experienced and famous teacher who was an old friend of Yefim Petrovitch. Ivan used to say later that it was all because of Yefim Petrovitch’s “ardor for good works.” Yefim Petrovitch was carried away by the idea that a boy of genius ought to be trained by a teacher of genius. But by the time the young man finished at the gymnasium and entered the university, neither Yefim Petrovitch nor this teacher was alive. Yefim Petrovitch had made no arrangement for paying out the tyrannical old lady’s legacy, which had grown from one thousand to two. The money was held up by the red tape that is unavoidable in Russia, and for his first two years at the university the young man was hard pressed, because he had to keep himself the whole time he was studying. It should be noted that he did not even try to contact his father. Perhaps this was pride, or contempt. Perhaps it was cool common sense, which told him he would get no real help from such a father. Whatever the reason, the young man was not at all downhearted, and he found work. At first he gave sixpenny lessons, and later he placed short items about street incidents in the newspapers, signed “Eye-Witness.” These items, it was said, were so lively and spicy that the papers soon took them. This alone showed the young man’s practical and intellectual superiority over the crowds of needy, unlucky students of both sexes who haunt the offices of newspapers and journals, unable to think of anything better than endless begging for copying work and translations from the French. Once Ivan Fyodorovitch had made contact with the editors, he always kept it up. In his later years at the university he published brilliant reviews of books on various specialized subjects, and became well known in literary circles. But only in his last year did he suddenly catch the attention of a much wider readership, so that a great many people noticed him and remembered him. It was a rather curious episode. He had just left the university and was getting ready to go abroad on his two thousand roubles, when Ivan Fyodorovitch published a strange article in one of the major journals. It attracted general notice. The subject was one he could have been supposed to know nothing about, since he was a student of natural science. It dealt with a question being debated everywhere at the time: the status of the ecclesiastical courts. After going through several opinions on the matter, he went on to give his own view. What struck people most about the article was its tone and its unexpected conclusion. Many in the Church party took him without question as one of their own. Yet the secularists, and even atheists, joined them in applauding him. In the end, some shrewd people suggested that the article was nothing but an impudent satirical burlesque. I mention this episode in particular because the article made its way into the famous monastery in our neighborhood. The monks there took a special interest in the question of the ecclesiastical courts, and the article left them completely bewildered. When they learned the author’s name, they were interested to find that he was a native of our town and the son of “that Fyodor Pavlovitch.” And just then the author himself showed up among us.
